metadata.title: Survey of Adult Skills 2023 – Country Notes: Chile

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The document reports results from the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 (Second Cycle) for Chile, based on a household survey with a personal interview and a self-completed digital assessment. The sample is described as representative of about 13.5 million adults aged 16–65 residing in Chile, with analyses including non-response bias checks. The country notes do not specify the exact survey weight variable names or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from this excerpt. For OECD/PIAAC-style adult skills reporting, analysts should use the official sampling/survey weights provided with the microdata to account for the complex survey design and non-response; if replicate weights are available, they should be used for uncertainty estimates (e.g., 95% confidence intervals shown in figures).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This country notes document reports descriptive proficiency levels and associations with outcomes, but it does not provide methodological details on plausible values (PV) generation/combination or any explicit missing-data handling procedure. The proficiency estimates are described as being on 500-point scales derived from task success/failure, and doorstep respondents’ proficiency is estimated from a statistical model using doorstep questionnaire information; however, the excerpt does not document the PV framework or missing-data strategy used in the underlying OECD production. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported for this extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is the set of adults aged 16–65 who participated in the Survey of Adult Skills 2022–23 in Chile (second participation). The document indicates that doorstep questionnaire respondents were offered when participants were not sufficiently fluent in the assessment language, and that doorstep respondents are generally excluded when comparing results across cycles to maximize comparability; the figures/notes also state that some analyses exclude doorstep-only respondents due to language barriers. For the reported proficiency and outcome figures, the document also specifies that employment and well-being/civic outcomes are for adults aged 25–65 not in formal education (and employment outcomes exclude doorstep-only respondents).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD country notes report summarizes Chile’s performance in the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 (Second Cycle), which assessed adults aged 16–65 in 31 countries/economies (Chile also assessed a sample of 15-year-olds). In Chile, mean proficiency is reported on 500-point scales for literacy (218), numeracy (214), and adaptive problem solving (218), each below the OECD average, with uncertainty shown via 95% confidence intervals. The report provides proficiency-level distributions (e.g., 53% at Level 1 or below in literacy; 56% at Level 1 or below in numeracy and adaptive problem solving) and highlights age-related gaps (older adults 55–65 scoring lower than 25–34). It also describes associations between skills and outcomes: higher numeracy is linked to better employment opportunities and wages (a one-standard-deviation increase in numeracy associated with 15% higher wages after accounting for other differences), and higher skills relate to life satisfaction, health, and trust. Methodological details on PV handling, missing data, and any ML modeling used for proficiency estimation are not provided in this excerpt, so the extraction focuses on reported descriptive and correlational results rather than predictive modeling.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive OECD country notes report rather than an empirical ML paper that trains and evaluates predictive models on microdata within the article text. As a result, there are no student-level ML algorithms, target variables, or model performance metrics to extract into main_findings. The document also does not report the technical details needed to classify PV handling and missing-data procedures beyond high-level descriptions of proficiency estimation and doorstep modeling.
